full_judgment:
2. This application arises out of an order passed by the District Judge, Chuadatiga, Meherpur on 24.2.85 di, missing the Misc. Election Tribunal Appeal No. 1 of 1985 which was directed against the order passed by the Munsif, Meherpur on 30 12 84 in Election Tribunal Misc. Case No. 8 of 1984. The learned Munsif being the Election Tribunal after recording the evidence before the parties passed an order for recounting of the votes of the ballot papers. As against that the opposite party No.1 preferred an appeal before the District Judge which has been dismissed. 

 4. It appears that the learned Munsif after perusing the evidence held that it was necessary to scrutinise and count the ballot papers in the interest or justice. The learned District Judge who heard the appeal also noticed that the evidence of the parties adduced in this case in which the respondent No. petitioner and his witnesses have categorically asserted that about 1.15 invalid votes of the. appellant opposite party No. 1 who got himself elected by a margin of 9 votes were treated as valid votes and many valid votes of respondent No. 1 petitioner as invalid by the Presiding Officer and assistant Presiding Officer "and he gave a finding in the following language" "In view of the assertion and, the allegation made in the election petition it cannot in any way be said that the learned Election Tribunal acted without his jurisdiction or rather to say that sufficient foundation was not laid to come to the fading that recounting was indispensably necessary for complete and effective adjudication of the election petition. The contrary contention of the learned Advocate of the appellant opposite party No. 1 is without any substance and is of no avail to him." 

 5. In this view of the matter the learned District Judge found that the Election Tribunal was justified in passing the impugned order for recounting of the ballot papers. In these circumstances of the case and for complete and effective adjudication of the election petition the Election Tribunal was justified in directing recounting. In this connection we may refer to the decision cited by Mr. Sharif reported in 27 DLR 594 in the case of Amizuddin Ahmed Vs. Election Tribunal where-in it was held: "The Election Rules do not provide for recounting ballot papers by the Tribunal and the power to recount ballot papers has been given under rule 41 to the Presiding Officer only. But if recounting of ballot papers is a material issue before the Tribunal and the election petition cannot be determined without such recounting, only then the Tribunal has got power to reopen the ballot boxes and recount the ballot papers in presence of parties. Before doing so it must come to a finding by evidence on oath that this recounting is indispensably necessary". 

 6. In the instant case several witnesses were examined in support of the allegation made in the Election petition to the effect that the counting was not made properly, on consideration of the evidence which were taken on oath before the Court the learned thought it proper to pass an order for recounting. Mr. Sharif has cited another decision reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 305 in the case of Manik Chowdhury Vs. Election Tribunal (Munsif, Sadar), Faridpur wherein it was held:- “Tribunal cannot recount votes to interfere with the election result unless a case of improper counting by the Presiding Officer is made out". 

 7. From the above decision also it appears that the Tribunal can pass an order for re-counting if he is satisfied with the evidence that improper counting was made by the Presiding Officer. In the instant case there are evidence on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 as to the incorrect counting of the votes and to that effect certain witnesses are examined. In that view of the matter the learned Munsif passed the order for recounting.
